utterance:
Good news: your examination is very reassuring. There's tenderness and muscle spasm in the muscles on the left side of your lower back, and no sign of any nerve being trapped — your legs are fully normal, with normal strength, feeling and reflexes. There are also no worrying features like fever, weight loss, or problems with your bladder or bowel.

This is almost certainly a strain or sprain of the muscles and ligaments in your lower back from the lifting. This is very common and usually settles well with time and staying active.
reply: Are you sure I do not need an MRI? I was really hoping for a scan to make sure I have not slipped a disc, and I am worried this is serious and want to know what is going on.

utterance:
That's a very reasonable thing to ask about, and I can see why you'd want it. Here's the honest picture: for most simple low back pain, an MRI doesn't help and can actually mislead. It often shows "abnormalities" — disc bulges, wear and tear — that many people with no pain at all also have, and that don't explain your symptoms. The key information comes from how you feel and what I've found on examination, and that tells me there is no nerve being compressed, which is what really matters.

If you had pain shooting down the leg, leg weakness, numbness, or trouble with your bladder or bowel, then a scan would be important and I'd arrange one straight away. You don't have any of those. So at this stage a scan isn't needed and wouldn't change what we do — the treatment is the same either way.

I'd suggest this: treat it properly for the next few weeks. If you're not improving in that time, or if anything new appears (like pain down the leg, numbness, or bladder/bowel changes), we'll reassess and I'll happily organise a scan then. How does that sound?
reply: I figured I would need an MRI to see what is going on, but if you are confident I do not need a scan right now, I suppose I can try to give it a couple of weeks to see if it improves.

awards.label: What he expects from the visit

utterance:
Thank you — I think that's the right approach. Here's my plan for you.

First, pain relief. Paracetamol alone hasn't helped much, so I'll add an anti-inflammatory to bring down the pain and muscle spasm — I'll prescribe some ibuprofen (or something similar) to take regularly for a few days, with or after food. Continue the paracetamol too if it helps.

Second, and importantly, keep moving. Don't stay lying on the couch all day — that actually slows recovery. Stay gently active: short walks several times a day, moving within what's comfortable. It's normal to feel some pain with movement; that doesn't mean you're causing damage. Continue your work as much as you can, and take short breaks to move rather than long spells of being still.

Keep using heat if it helps. Avoid heavy lifting, twisting and bending for a couple of weeks while it settles.
reply: Okay, I will take the ibuprofen and try to stay moving with short walks instead of lying on the couch, even though I am still worried about how much it hurts to move.

utterance:
That's understandable to be worried, but being cautious with movement while staying gently active is exactly right — you don't need to push through severe pain, just keep moving within what's tolerable.

A couple of important things to watch for. Please come back sooner, or seek urgent care, if any of these develop:
- pain, numbness or tingling going down one or both legs,
- any weakness in your legs or difficulty walking,
- any new trouble passing urine or stool, or loss of feeling/control in your bladder or bowel, or numbness around your back passage or genitals,
- fever, or feeling generally unwell,
- or if the pain simply gets worse despite treatment.

For most people this settles over two to six weeks. I'd like to see you again in about two to three weeks to check how you're going. If it's still significantly limiting you at that point, that's when we'd reconsider a scan or further input. Does all this make sense, and do you have any questions?
reply: It makes sense, but honestly, I have been reading about slipped discs and people needing surgery, so I am still a bit worried about that.

awards.label: What he is worried the pain might be

utterance:
I completely understand that worry — the internet can paint a scary picture. Let me reassure you. A "slipped disc" only becomes a problem if it presses on a nerve, and the nerve to your legs shows absolutely no sign of being compressed: you have no pain down the leg, no numbness, no weakness, and my examination was entirely normal. When those nerves aren't affected, disc problems don't cause harm and don't need surgery — in fact, the vast majority of people with a bulging disc recover fully without any operation, just with time and staying active.

Surgery is only ever needed in a small minority, and those are people with severe nerve symptoms or bladder/bowel trouble — none of which you have. So I'm confident surgery is not on the horizon for you. If anything changes and those symptoms do appear, we act on it quickly. Try not to worry, and follow the plan. How are you feeling about it now?
reply: That actually reassures me a fair bit to hear that I do not have those nerve symptoms and that surgery is not something I need to worry about. I will follow the plan and stick to the short walks and the ibuprofen.

awards.label: Ibuprofen 400 mg orally three times daily with food, short course

utterance:
I've written the prescription for ibuprofen 400 mg, three times a day for a week, always with or after food to protect your stomach. If you notice any stomach pain, indigestion or heartburn, stop it and let me know. I'll also add a medicine to protect your stomach if needed.

So to summarise: ibuprofen regularly for a week (plus paracetamol if helpful), gentle short walks to keep moving, avoid heavy lifting and twisting, and watch for the warning signs I mentioned. See me in two to three weeks. Take care, and don't hesitate to come back sooner if anything worries you.
reply: Thank you, Doctor. I appreciate you taking the time to explain everything clearly and for reassuring me.
